## Stage fright
Stage fright or performance anxiety is the anxiety, fear, or persistent phobia that may be aroused in an individual by the requirement to perform in front of an audience, real or imagined, whether actually or potentially (for example, when performing before a camera). Performing in front of an unknown audience can cause significantly more anxiety than performing in front of familiar faces. Conversely, some performers report minimal anxiety when appearing before strangers, but severe stage fright when friends, family, and colleagues are present. This condition can manifest up to 36 hours beforehand, with classic symptoms such as nausea, dry mouth, and eye twitches.
In some cases, stage fright may be a part of a larger pattern of social phobia (social anxiety disorder), but many people experience stage fright without any wider problems. Quite often, stage fright arises from the mere anticipation of a performance, often long before it happens. It has numerous manifestations: stuttering, tachycardia, tremor in the hands and legs, sweaty hands, facial nerve tics, dry mouth, and dizziness.

plan.title: Calm Before You Speak: A Guide to Presentation Anxiety
plan.description: A practical guide to performance anxiety, covering why stage fright happens in the body, how breathing and preparation can help, and when to seek professional support. It is general information, not medical advice.

beats.narration: Your heart pounds, your hands shake, and you haven't even stood up yet. Why does a simple presentation feel like an attack? Your body is not broken. It is doing its job.
beats.chapter: Why your body panics before you speak

beats.narration: Stage fright, also called performance anxiety, is fear triggered by having to perform in front of an audience, whether that audience is real or only imagined.

props.definition: Anxiety or fear triggered by having to perform in front of an audience, real or imagined.

beats.narration: Here is the chain. The audience seems risky. Then your brain's alarm fires. Adrenaline floods your body, preparing it to fight or run, as if you faced real danger.
That surge explains the signs: a racing heart, trembling hands or legs, sweaty palms, a dry mouth, nausea, dizziness, even stuttering or facial tics.
It can begin up to 36 hours beforehand. Often it starts from mere anticipation, long before you walk into the room.

props.label: Stage fright can start this long before a performance

beats.narration: The audience matters, too. For some people, strangers raise anxiety the most. Others feel fine with strangers, but worse in front of friends, family or colleagues.
Here is the reassuring part. Many people have stage fright without any wider problem. Sometimes it is part of social anxiety disorder, which we will come back to.

props.text: Stage fright is a normal alarm, not a personal flaw.

beats.narration: So what can you actually do? Start with your breath. Breathe in gently through your nose, then make the exhale longer than the inhale, as if slowly fogging a window.

steps.label: Breathe in gently through your nose

beats.narration: Stanford researchers found that five minutes of exhale-focused breathing, called cyclic sighing, improved mood and slowed breathing more than mindfulness meditation. Another study found that the exact ratio mattered little. Slowing down is what helps.

props.heading: How strong is the evidence?
items: Five minutes of cyclic sighing eased mood
Exact breath ratio: no clear difference

beats.narration: When it works, your breathing slows, your shoulders drop, and your thoughts feel a little quieter. Practice when you are calm, so the skill is ready when you need it.
Use it in two places. In the hours before, give it five minutes. Just before you start, take a few slow breaths.
Rehearse out loud, not just in your head. Try an empty room that looks like the real setting, then a friendly listener. Practicing alone never tests the fear of being watched.

image_queries: person practicing speech in front of friend
props.alt: rehearsing a presentation in realistic settings

beats.narration: Know your opening lines by heart, because anxiety peaks at the start. Memorize your opening lines. Then let your body settle as you speak.

Finally, reframe the signals. A pounding heart means your body is getting ready, not that you are failing. In one Harvard study, people who said "I am excited" spoke more persuasively than those who tried to calm down.

props.text: A fast heart means you are getting ready, not failing.

beats.narration: Nerves before a talk are normal. But how do you know when it's become something more? Some signs are worth noticing, and they have little to do with how loud your heart beats.

props.title: When nerves become something more
props.subtitle: Knowing when to ask for professional help

beats.narration: Watch for avoidance, like calling in sick to dodge a presentation. Notice worry that starts weeks ahead, or lingers long after. And ask whether it is hurting your work, school, or daily life.

props.heading: Signs it may be more than nerves
items: Worry for weeks before or long after
Hurting your work, school or daily life

beats.narration: Sometimes stage fright is part of social anxiety disorder. Shyness is a personality trait. Social anxiety is a diagnosable condition, with persistent, intense fear. The good news is that it is treatable.

Avoiding the situation may feel better today, but according to Mayo Clinic, anxiety is likely to continue long term without treatment. Getting help early matters, because anxiety can be harder to treat if you wait.

props.text: Avoiding feels better today, but the anxiety tends to stay.

beats.narration: Who can you ask? Start with a GP or doctor. They know many people struggle with this. They can refer you to a therapist, and ask about cognitive behavioural therapy, called CBT.
A meta-analysis of 25 trials found CBT for social anxiety brought lasting improvement, twelve months or longer after treatment ended. This is general information, not medical advice.

props.label: CBT gains for social anxiety lasted 12 months or longer

beats.narration: Get urgent help for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or thoughts of self-harm. Contact emergency services or a crisis line. Support exists, and you don't have to face it alone.
So here is your next step. Pick one technique from this video, and practise it before your next talk. And if anxiety keeps holding you back, reach out. Asking for help is a strong move.

accuracy.reason: Mostly sound, but "Harvard study" (the excitement study was Alison Wood Brooks at Harvard Business School, while the cited source is an APA release) and the "25 trials" meta-analysis are not in the notes. The six-word line "Stanford researchers found... more than mindfulness meditation" is true but "Another study found ratio mattered little" is loosely sourced. The claim that anxiety peaks at the start is unsupported.

coverage.reason: Covers physiology, breathing, rehearsal, reframing and when to seek help, but there is no physiological sigh or box breathing, no exposure practice, and little on beta blockers or on the cognitive side. Too much time goes to the unknown-versus-familiar audience trivia.

structure.reason: Three clear chapters and a logical order, but the physiology section is bloated while preparation is rushed. Beat 13 repeats itself and the "36 hours" and audience beats are digressions.

hook_ending.reason: Opens with a relatable physical image and the line "Your body is not broken. It is doing its job." The ending gives one concrete next step plus encouragement, though it is slightly generic.

tone.reason: Compassionate, non-diagnostic, reassuring, with a disclaimer included. Mild US mismatch with "GP" and "behavioural".

visuals.reason: Good variety (diagram, steps, versus, timeline, gallery, stat). The stat "25 trials" is a weak stat, the versus table for audience type is clumsy, and the final title scene shows a sentence fragment as the title.

originality.reason: The fogging-a-window image and the avoidance example (calling in sick) are nice touches, but much of the content is standard advice.

instructions.reason: Hits all four requested areas, but the breathing section is thin on specific techniques and is under-practical; the length is roughly right.

language.reason: Generally fluent, but with a redundant line ("Know your opening lines by heart... Memorize your opening lines."), UK spellings ("practise", "behavioural") for a US viewer, and the odd "Own your first moments".

defects.quote: Know your opening lines by heart, because anxiety peaks at the start. Memorize your opening lines.
defects.issue: Redundant repetition; the peak-at-start claim is unsourced.

defects.quote: In one Harvard study, people who said "I am excited" spoke more persuasively
defects.issue: Not in the notes; the cited source is APA, and attribution and the persuasiveness finding are from memory. The study was by Brooks at Harvard Business School, so the attribution is loosely right but unverified.

defects.quote: A meta-analysis of 25 trials found CBT for social anxiety brought lasting improvement
defects.issue: Specific figure not in the notes; it cannot be traced.

defects.quote: Breathe in gently through your nose, then make the exhale longer than the inhale
defects.issue: Offers a generic technique but omits the physiological sigh or box breathing named in a good answer, plus exposure practice.

defects.quote: The audience matters, too. For some people, strangers raise anxiety the most.
defects.issue: Trivia digression that uses time better spent on preparation tactics.

defects.quote: Start with a GP or doctor.
defects.issue: UK phrasing for a US viewer (say primary care doctor); "behavioural" is also UK.

defects.quote: So here is your next step. Pick one technique
defects.issue: A sentence fragment used as the title card with an empty subtitle.

missing: Gradual exposure and practice in low-stakes settings
Beta blockers or medication mention and talking to a doctor
Focusing on the audience or message rather than yourself
Normalizing a shaky start and pausing
wrong_facts: "Harvard study" and "25 trials" are not in the notes (unverified, but plausibly true).
"anxiety peaks at the start" is unsupported by the notes.
judge.summary: A compassionate, well-organized script that covers the basics but is thin on practical technique, spends time on trivia, and relies on a few unsourced specifics. It needs sharper breathing and preparation content and tighter wording.
